title: Taiwan Reports 83% Surge in Chinese Vessel Activity Near Island
excerpt: Coast guard data shows 55 Chinese government vessel sightings around Taiwan in June, up from 30 in May, as Taipei plans drills to counter potential blockade of Pacific supply routes.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Taiwan recorded 55 Chinese vessel sightings in June, an 83% increase from May.
  • Taipei plans joint drills to counter potential Chinese blockade of Pacific supply routes.
  • Chinese coast guard vessels now patrol in pairs near Taiwan's exclusive economic zone.
  • A blockade could cost global GDP $2 trillion annually and disrupt India's semiconductor exports.

Year-on-Year Increase (%)
Taiwan Coast Guard data
  • Taiwan detected 55 Chinese coast guard and research vessel sightings around the island in June, an 83% increase from May and 120% rise year-on-year.
  • Taipei officials say Beijing may be rehearsing how to sever Taiwan's Pacific supply lines, prompting plans for joint coast guard-navy drills.
  • Chinese coast guard vessels, including former naval destroyers, now regularly patrol in pairs outside Taiwan's exclusive economic zone in the Pacific.
  • A potential Taiwan blockade could trigger a $2 trillion annual hit to global GDP and severely disrupt semiconductor exports to India.

Taiwan detected a sharp rise in Chinese coast guard and research vessel activity around the island in June, with sightings jumping 83% from the previous month, according to Taiwan Coast Guard data released on Sunday. The escalation has prompted Taipei to plan live drills simulating Chinese moves to cut off its Pacific lifeline routes.

The coast guard recorded 55 Chinese government vessel sightings — including coast guard and research boats — around Taiwan in June, up from 30 in May, according to Reuters. The figure marked a 120% increase from 25 sightings recorded in June last year. The tally excluded sightings around Taiwan-controlled islands near the Chinese coast.

Coast Guard as a Tool of Pressure

While China's military has operated almost daily around Taiwan for years, Beijing has increasingly turned to its coast guard to assert territorial claims in what Taipei calls "lawfare" — efforts to create a legal basis for Chinese jurisdiction around the island. The figures underscore the coast guard's growing role in Beijing's pressure campaign, which has drawn alarm from the United States, Britain, France and Germany.

“If the situation escalates to a blockade — or what would already amount to a quasi-war — we have plans to work with the navy to jointly protect Taiwan’s lifeline sea routes.”

— Senior Taiwan Coast Guard official

"Nearly 50% of global container shipping transits the Taiwan Strait, and a blockade scenario would disrupt semiconductor exports critical to India's growing electronics and automotive sectors."

"Nearly 50% of global container shipping transits the Taiwan Strait, and a blockade scenario would disrupt semiconductor exports critical to India's growing electronics and automotive sectors."

A senior coast guard official told reporters that some Chinese coast guard ships are former naval destroyers that have been repainted for coast guard use, giving them military-grade capabilities in terms of size, endurance and weapons systems. These vessels now regularly operate in pairs just outside Taiwan's exclusive economic zone in the Pacific, stretching Taipei's limited coast guard fleet.

Questioning Commercial Shipping

In a particularly provocative move, Chinese coast guard vessels have begun broadcasting questions to merchant ships about their port entry and exit information, effectively pressuring commercial shipping even though no vessel has changed course so far, officials said. Taiwan has responded by broadcasting back, telling ships to maintain normal navigation and ignore the Chinese interference.

“It knows it has no jurisdiction now, so it is trying to create something out of nothing,” a second senior Taiwan official said, describing the activity as an “expansion” aimed at changing the status quo.

Wider Military Buildup

The coast guard data arrives against a backdrop of broader Chinese military escalation. Taiwan National Security Bureau Director-General Tsai Ming-yen told lawmakers earlier this month that the July-to-September period is the peak season for Chinese military exercises, and that the mobilisation of naval and maritime forces has shown an “upward trend” this year.

As of early July, Taiwan was tracking more than 110 Chinese military and coast guard ships deployed along the First Island Chain — a strategic arc stretching from Japan through Taiwan to the Philippines — according to Joseph Wu, secretary-general of Taiwan's National Security Council. Wu called the deployments “a clear sign of expansionism.”

In June, China also deployed a six-ship flotilla 140 nautical miles east of Taiwan in what it called a “special maritime law enforcement operation,” according to USNI News. The operation, which involved coast guard cutters and maritime safety patrol ships, came in response to maritime boundary talks between the Philippines and Japan.

What a Blockade Would Mean for India

For the Indian diaspora and India's economy, the stakes are considerable. Nearly 50% of global container shipping transits the Taiwan Strait, and a blockade scenario would disrupt semiconductor exports critical to India's growing electronics and automotive sectors. The Rhodium Group has estimated that a Taiwan blockade would cause $2 trillion in annual global economic losses — roughly 3% of world GDP.

Taiwan's trade relationship with India has deepened in recent years, with Taiwanese foreign direct investment in India exceeding $665 million in the five years to 2023. Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing, a Taiwanese firm, has partnered with India's Tata Group to build the country's first semiconductor fabrication facility in Gujarat. Any disruption to Taiwan’s supply chains would ripple directly through India's manufacturing, IT services and e-commerce sectors.

Impact of a Potential Blockade
›Blockade could disrupt 50% of global container shipping.

›Critical semiconductor exports to India at risk.

What’s Next

Taiwan's coast guard is planning live drills simulating Chinese escalations off its Pacific coast, with coordination from the navy. China's defence ministry and Taiwan Affairs Office have not responded to requests for comment. With the peak exercise season running through September and Chinese-Russian joint naval drills also underway near Qingdao, regional tensions show no signs of easing. Analysts will be watching whether Beijing escalates from coast guard patrols to more overt military action — and whether Taiwan's allies respond with concrete countermeasures.
